title: The third-time rule
teaser: How to decide which knowledge needs to leave someone's head and become a short training.
body:
The first time someone asks you how to do something, answer.

The second time, answer again. People forget. That's fine.

The third time, stop answering and start capturing.

That's the rule I use to decide which knowledge has to leave someone's head and become a micro-training: a 1-minute video, a checklist, a one-page guide.

Why the third time?

One question is a moment. Three is a pattern. And a pattern means the next ten people will ask the same thing.

Most organizations try to document everything at once and end up with a wiki nobody reads. The third-time rule does the opposite: it captures only what people actually need, in the order they need it.

What's the question you've answered three times this month?

title: Don't ask AI to write the training. Ask it to interview the expert
teaser: One prompt that draws out the steps your expert no longer sees.
body:
The hardest part of building training isn't writing it. It's getting the knowledge out of the expert's head.

Experts skip steps they've done a thousand times. Not on purpose. They just don't see them anymore.

So flip it. Don't ask AI to write the training. Ask it to interview the expert.

Try this prompt

You are an instructional designer. Interview me about how I do [task]. Ask one question at a time. Push for the steps I might skip, the mistakes beginners make, and the moments where I make a judgment call. After 10 questions, summarize the process as a step-by-step outline.

Ten minutes later you have what a blank page never gives you: the hidden steps.

The expert brings the knowledge. AI brings the questions. You bring the structure.

title: Your onboarding isn't too short. It's too heavy
teaser: Why 80 pages of procedures don't stick, and what works better.
body:
Day one: a stack of procedures to read. Day two: shadowing. Day three: "Any questions?"

Nobody remembers 80 pages of procedures. Not after two days, and not after three months.

The fix isn't shorter content. It's a different order.

What works better is almost boring

  1. One small, real task.
  2. Only the knowledge needed to do that task.
  3. Do it in the field, then get feedback.
  4. Then the next task.

People learn from doing, not from reading binders. Micro-learning isn't about cutting a 60-minute module into six 10-minute ones. It's about sequencing knowledge in the order the work actually happens.

How to start

List the first five tasks a new hire really does. For each one, ask what they need to know before they can do it, and nothing more. That list is your onboarding plan.

title: A procedure without the headache
teaser: Three steps from a phone recording to an organized work guide.
body:
Need to write a procedure or a guide and can't face starting from a blank page?

  1. Start a recording on your phone and explain the process, step by step.
  2. Upload the recording to your AI tool and ask for a transcript.
  3. Ask: "Turn this into an organized work guide, in clear bullet points."

Within a minute or two you have an outline, and you build from there.

title: The productivity illusion
teaser: We were promised AI would save us time. So why are we all working more?
body:
We were promised AI would save us time. So why are we all working more?

If a presentation used to take two days, today people expect three in a day. The technology really does save time, but the market's standard just jumped up.

The most critical skill now isn't doing things faster. It's knowing how to set boundaries and choose what not to spend your time on.

title: When everything depends on one employee
teaser: It looks like an asset. In practice, it's a risk.
body:
Do you have one employee everyone turns to?

It looks like an asset. In practice, it's a risk. When all the knowledge and experience is buried with one person, everyone queues up at their desk and the business depends on them.

The goal isn't to clone the person. The goal is to turn their knowledge into a system: simple decision aids in the field that let more people reach the same level of performance.

title: Slides that put people to sleep? Here's the fix
teaser: Three simple rules for every slide.
body:
40 slides, a million lines, a tiny font. We've all sat through a training like that.

The simplest trick to upgrade any presentation

  1. One key message per slide.
  2. An image or icon that supports it.
  3. Three standout words, no more.

And most important: your slides aren't your teleprompter. They're the set and the support for what you have to say.
